title: The Origins of Some Everyday Superstitions
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the origins of everyday superstitions, including why humans are superstitious (desire for control, pattern-seeking, placebo and survival instincts), horseshoes and the devil legend, wishbone breaking from the Etruscans onward, spilling salt and the Last Supper, rabbit's foot charms and West African folk magic (hoodoo), walking under ladders and the Trinity, stepping on cracks, and knocking on wood. The episode closes with a listener mail correction from the American Association of Poison Control Centers about the poison helpline web address (poison help dot org).

entities.name: American Association of Poison Control Centers

segments.title: Opening banter and superstition intro
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about their own superstitions, such as knocking on wood, avoiding the number four, and throwing salt at ladders. They introduce the premise that humans are superstitious from a desire to control the world.

segments.title: Why we are superstitious
segments.summary: The hosts discuss pattern-seeking and cause-and-effect, a placebo-like effect where rituals affect the person performing them, and evolutionary survival instincts that become superstition when omens such as a full moon are added.

segments.title: Horseshoes and the devil legend
segments.summary: The hosts tell an Irish legend in which a blacksmith nails a hot horseshoe to the devil's hoof, and link it to hanging horseshoes over doors. They explain that iron and crescent shapes were considered lucky, and discuss whether horseshoes should hang heels up or down.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break; the hosts mention a Journal of American Folklore article on horseshoes.

segments.title: Wishbone breaking
segments.summary: The hosts explain how the furcula (wishbone) is broken to make a wish, tracing the custom to the Etruscans, who saw birds as oracles, then to the Romans and Britain, where a longer rule-based version developed. They note the phrase 'lucky break' origin is disputed, and mention the bone in dinosaurs.

segments.title: Spilling salt and the Last Supper
segments.summary: The hosts discuss throwing spilled salt over the left shoulder, linked to Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, where Judas is shown knocking over salt. They also note that salt was historically valuable and that spilling it was seen as wasteful.

segments.title: Rabbit's foot charm and hoodoo
segments.summary: The hosts discuss rabbit's foot keychains and their association with fertility and the underworld. They describe hoodoo beliefs from West African folk magic, in which a rabbit's left rear foot taken from a witch-rabbit shot with a silver bullet in a graveyard at midnight is especially lucky. They also share an anecdote about Booker T. Washington.

segments.title: Walking under a ladder and undoing bad luck
segments.summary: The hosts explain the Holy Trinity explanation for avoiding walking under ladders, the gallows and Egyptian theories, and ways to undo bad luck such as wishing, walking back through, spitting, the fig sign, saying bread and butter, and crossing fingers until seeing a dog.

segments.title: Stepping on cracks and knocking on wood
segments.summary: Chuck describes his habit of balancing cracks he steps on. The hosts cover the rhyme about breaking your mother's back and the idea that cracks lead to the underworld, and finish with the Celtic origin of knocking on wood.

segments.title: Listener mail: poison control correction and outro
segments.summary: A listener mail correction from the American Association of Poison Control Centers: the web address for the poison helpline triage tool is poison help dot org, not poison dot org. The hosts thank them and sign off.
